$schema-note: Hand-maintained. Data, not code: nothing under src/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for the `tools` half of this package — the ten canonical
rows ADR M0.3 §1 row 7 gives that context, written from here because ADR
M0.3 §15 gives the ORM one home and `CANONICAL_STORE_ADAPTERS` in
scripts/arch/table-ownership.mjs delegates them to this directory. One
entry per tenant clause, transaction boundary, driver-error mapping and
ordering rule, each carrying the file it lives in, the EXACT text that
implements it (`from`), the edit that removes it (`to`), why it is load-
bearing (`why`), and the NAMED cases that were SEEN to go red (`kills`).
FIFTEEN OF THE FIFTEEN NEED A REAL POSTGRESQL OR A REAL DRIVER, and none
could have been written against the in-memory double. The double compares
`resolvePath(scope)` against the one scope it was constructed with, so it
cannot tell a forged ancestry from a deleted environment; it has no
json-root CHECK, no NULL-distinct unique index, no ancestry trigger and no
planner to return rows in an order nothing pinned.
TEN OF THE SIXTEEN SURVIVED WHEN THE SWEEP FIRST RAN, AND THAT IS THE
REASON THIS FILE EXISTS. M01, M02, M03, M04, M06, M08, M09, M13, M14 and
M16 all survived against the five suites this tranche shipped: the store
passed with its ancestry resolve blind to the organization, with an
unknown environment admitted, with `replaceExposures` deleting another
entity's rows, with the enable's tenant clause gone and with two orderings
reversed. Six kills out of sixteen is not a store that is well tested; it
is a store whose guards nothing could contradict.
`tools-isolation.integration.test.ts` (eight cases) and the four `what a
throw becomes` cases in `tools-mapping.test.ts` were written to close
exactly those, and the SECOND sweep is what the entries below record: 15
killed, 1 survived, 0 vacuous, on a baseline of 57 green cases. The one
survivor is recorded under `unfalsifiable` rather than deleted.
procedure: PROVE THE SUITES GREEN FIRST. Tranche 1's first sweep reported 22 kills
and every one was VACUOUS: the context's dist/ had been cleaned, so every
suite failed to LOAD and 'died' against no mutation at all. The driver
used here runs the suite set UNMUTATED and refuses to sweep unless it is
green, and classifies a run in which NO CASE EXECUTED as VACUOUS rather
than as a kill. The baseline for the run recorded here was 57 cases, 0
`from` with its `to` in the named file; run `pnpm exec vitest run tools-`
from this package with DOCKER_HOST and
TESTCONTAINERS_DOCKER_SOCKET_OVERRIDE set; confirm a NAMED case in `kills`
fails; restore the file. An anchor that matches zero times or more than

unfalsifiable.name: M09 exposures: the exposure ordering stops being TOTAL
unfalsifiable.verdict: SURVIVED — recorded rather than hidden, and NOT counted as a guard
why: The exposure order is guarded TWICE and either guard alone is enough,
so removing one is not observable. `readExposures` orders in SQL and
`.sort(byExposureOrder)` the rows again in JS. Truncating the SQL
`ORDER BY` to its first term leaves every one of those three answering
identically, because the JS sort is total.
The one method that CAN see it is `pageExposures`, which sorts after
the database has already chosen the page — so a non-total SQL order
decides WHICH rows are on it. Ties are needed to expose that, and on
this fixture PostgreSQL returns tied rows in a stable order anyway, so
a case written against it would assert planner behaviour rather than a
property of this store and would pass for the wrong reason.
REPORTED AS A REDUNDANCY, NOT CLOSED WITH A CASE THAT WOULD NOT MEAN
WHAT IT SAID. The honest statement is that the SQL ordering is load-
bearing for `pageExposures` alone and is not independently falsifiable
here; a paging determinism proof needs a fixture built to produce ties

mutations.name: M01 scope: the ancestry check drops its ORGANIZATION half
mutations.why: The port note the double cannot honour: a scope is an organization, a project AND a leaf, so a `where` built on the leaf alone reads an environment that has since been re-parented. Only a real tree can state it.
kills: tools-isolation.integration.test.ts > the ancestry the scope claims, resolved against the real tree an environment under ANOTHER organization is refused, and the leaf is real

mutations.name: M02 scope: an environment that does not exist is PERMITTED
mutations.why: A forged ancestry and a deleted environment are two different operator problems. The double holds no tree and raises one refusal for both; this store mints two, and the pair is only meaningful if each is reachable.
kills: tools-isolation.integration.test.ts > the ancestry the scope claims, resolved against the real tree an environment that does not exist is a DIFFERENT refusal from a forged one

mutations.name: M03 scope: a TransactionScopeError is swallowed into a Result
mutations.from: if (error instanceof Error && error.name === "TransactionScopeError") throw error;
mutations.why: A `TransactionScopeError` means a write ran outside its unit of work. Folding it into a `Result` would let a write that never ran read as a store that was busy.
kills: tools-mapping.test.ts > what a throw becomes on the way out of the store a TransactionScopeError is RE-THROWN, never folded into a Result

mutations.name: M04 scope: driverCode loses the class-name fallback
mutations.from:
const name = (error as { readonly name?: unknown }).name;
  return typeof name === "string" ? name : "unknown";
mutations.why: A client-side validation error carries no `code`. Falling back to the literal `unknown` made a constraint the database refused and a bug in this package read identically.
kills: tools-mapping.test.ts > what a throw becomes on the way out of the store a CLIENT-SIDE validation error carries no code, so the refusal names its CLASS

mutations.name: M05 exposures: the bindings fold resolves the scope a SECOND time
mutations.to:
const bound = await catalogue.listAgentPolicyBindings(scope);
    return bound.ok ? bound.value : [];
mutations.why: `requireScope` is one statement on the front of every scoped method. Reaching for the public reader inside a fold already inside `inScope` pays it twice, on the hot path of every turn.
kills: tools-statements.integration.test.ts > statement counts the whole exposure matrix costs the same for 2 tools and for 20

mutations.name: M06 exposures: the replace DELETE loses its entity clause
mutations.why: `replaceExposures` deletes anything absent from the declaration. Keyed on the environment and the tool set alone it takes ANOTHER entity's rows with it, and every value it returns is still correct.
kills: tools-isolation.integration.test.ts > what one entity's registration may reach re-registering ONE entity leaves the other entity's exposures alone

mutations.name: M07 exposures: the createMany stops skipping duplicates
mutations.why: The update-then-create pair is only safe because the unique key lets the create skip a row the update already touched.
kills: tools-conformance.integration.test.ts > the shared conformance scenario the postgres adapter and the in-memory double answer it identically
tools-transaction.integration.test.ts > the transaction boundary, proved by failure injection when the CREATE of replaceExposures fails, the DELETE it already made is gone too

mutations.name: M08 exposures: setExposureEnabled loses its tenant clause
mutations.why: `updateMany` rather than `update`, because the tenant clause has to be IN the statement: `update` addresses the primary key alone, so an exposure id from another environment would be switched off by whoever guessed it.
kills: tools-isolation.integration.test.ts > what one entity's registration may reach an exposure id from another environment cannot be switched off

mutations.name: M10 transcript: saveCall stops checking the step is in scope
mutations.why: `ToolCall` has no tenant column at all — its ancestry is Step -> Turn -> Thread — so the step-in-scope read is the only thing standing between a caller and another environment's transcript.
kills: tools-constraints.integration.test.ts > constraints that exist only in the migrations a step in another environment is refused, and it is not the same refusal

mutations.from: return (value === null || value === undefined ? TENANCY_JSON_DB_NULL : value) as never;
mutations.why: A plain `null` for a nullable `Json` column is a client validation error, and the client's other sentinel stores the JSON scalar `null`, which the json-root CHECK refuses. Both are invisible against the double.

mutations.name: M12 audit-rows: writeResult stops wrapping a SCALAR result
mutations.why: The json-root CHECK admits only an object or an array, and a call's `result` is `unknown`. A scalar has to be wrapped on the way in and unwrapped on the way out, or it cannot be stored at all.

mutations.name: M13 transcript: listStepCalls returns the transcript BACKWARDS
mutations.why: A transcript read out of order is a transcript. Nothing about the values says which way round they should be.

mutations.name: M14 transcript: saveCall's update REWRITES the step and the instant
mutations.why: A call belongs to the step it was made in. Letting a later write move `stepId` or `createdAt` rewrites history, and the status update it rides on still lands, so no returned value looks wrong.

mutations.name: M15 exposures: the DELETE runs AFTER the writes, not before
mutations.why: The delete runs FIRST so a re-registration that drops one tool and adds another cannot transiently hold both.
kills: tools-conformance.integration.test.ts > the shared conformance scenario the postgres adapter and the in-memory double answer it identically

mutations.name: M16 transcript: findHealth stops pinning a deterministic row
mutations.why: `entityExternalId` is nullable and the unique index is NULL-DISTINCT, so two health rows for one (environment, tool) both stand. Without an ORDER BY the row a fold reads is whichever the planner returned.
kills: tools-isolation.integration.test.ts > the health row a NULL entity may hold twice findHealth pins the LOWEST id when two rows match, not an arbitrary one
